# Start the JDK Flight Recorder (JFR)

There are several ways to start the JFR and collect insights about a given Java
application, such as:

- [Using JDK Mission Control (JMC)](#start-jfr-using-jdk-mission-control-jmc)
- [Using `jcmd`](#start-jfr-using-jcmd)
- [During application start time](#start-jfr-when-starting-the-application)
- [Programmatically](#start-jfr-programmatically)
- [Using Java Management Service (JMS)](#start-jfr-through-java-management-service-jms)

## Prerequisites

- [Oracle Java 25](https://www.oracle.com/java/technologies/downloads/#java25)

- [JDK Mission Control (JMC)](https://www.oracle.com/java/technologies/javase/products-jmc9-downloads.html)

## JDK Mission Control (JMC)

1. Download the latest version of JMC from
   [here](https://www.oracle.com/java/technologies/javase/products-jmc9-downloads.html)

2. Specify the version of Java

   When having multiple versions of Java installed, you may need to specify
   which one to be used by JMC. This can be done through the `jmc.ini` file,
   found under the `Eclipse` directory of where JMC is installed.

   Add the `-vm` option followed by the path to the `bin` directory, as shown
   next.

   ```
   ...
   -vm
   /Users/aattard/.sdkman/candidates/java/current/bin
   ...
   ```

   Please note that this file will contain other information, which is excluded
   for brevity.

## Build the application

The following examples require the application to be built.

```shell
./mvnw clean package
```

(*Optional*) Verify that the JAR file was created

```shell
tree --sort=name './target/libs'
```

There should be one JAR file

```
./target/libs
└── start-jfr-1.0.0.jar

1 directory, 1 file
```

Some of the following commands dump JFR files into a `jfr` directory. Make sure
that the `jfr` directory exists.

```shell
rm -rf './jfr'
mkdir -p './jfr'
```

## Start JFR using JDK Mission Control (JMC)

1. Start the application

   While it is not important to run the application in the background, it’s
   convenient as you don’t have to switch to another terminal window.

   ```shell
   java -jar './target/libs/start-jfr-1.0.0.jar' > './target/start-jfr-jmc.log' 2>&1 &

   # Save the PID so later steps can reuse it after this entry finishes.
   echo "$!" > './target/start-jfr-jmc.pid'
   ```

   The application will run until interrupted (killed).

2. Open the JDK Mission Control

   ```shell
   jmc
   ```

3. Find the application

   ![Find application](./assets/images/JMC%20-%20Find%20application.png)

4. Expand the *Flight Recorder* node and double-click on the recordings child
   node

   ![Start recording](./assets/images/JMC%20-%20Start%20recording%201.png)

   Select the *Time fixed recording* option, and enter the duration. `30 s` is
   more than enough for this example.

   ![Start recording](./assets/images/JMC%20-%20Start%20recording%202.png)

   Click *Finish* to start the JFR recording.

5. Wait for the recording to complete

   ![Wait for recording to finish](./assets/images/JMC%20-%20Wait%20for%20recording%20to%20finish.png)

6. View the recording

   ![View recording](./assets/images/JMC%20-%20View%20recording.png)

7. Close the application when ready

   No need to keep the application running once the dump has been generated.

   ```shell
   kill "$(cat './target/start-jfr-jmc.pid')"
   ```

## Start JFR using `jcmd`

1. Start the application

   While it is not important to run the application in the background, it’s
   convenient as you don’t have to switch to another terminal window.

   ```shell
   java -jar './target/libs/start-jfr-1.0.0.jar' > './target/start-jfr-jcmd.log' 2>&1 &

   # Save the PID so later steps can reuse it after this entry finishes.
   echo "$!" > './target/start-jfr-jcmd.pid'
   ```

   The application will run until interrupted (killed).

2. (*Optional*) Identify the Java application PID

   ```shell
   jcmd
   ```

   This lists all Java applications running on this machine, including the
   `jcmd` command.

   ```
   123457 jdk.jcmd/sun.tools.jcmd.JCmd
   123456 ./target/libs/start-jfr-1.0.0.jar
   ```

   The PID for this application can be obtained using the following set of
   chained commands

   ```shell
   cat './target/start-jfr-jcmd.pid'
   ```

   This will print just the PID

   ```
   123456
   ```

3. Start JFR using `jcmd`

   Note how the previous command is used to obtain the PID for this Java
   application and then pass it to the `jcmd` command to start JFR.

   ```shell
   PID="$(cat './target/start-jfr-jcmd.pid')"
   jcmd "${PID}" \
     JFR.start \
     name='Start-JFR' \
     duration=30s \
     filename='./jfr/demo-jcmd.jfr'
   ```

   This will print just the PID and a message saying that the recording has
   started.

   ```
   123456:
   Started recording 1. The result will be written to:

   ./jfr/demo-jcmd.jfr
   ```

   Instead of `$(jcmd | grep 'start-jfr-1.0.0.jar' | cut -d' ' -f1)`, you can
   use the PID directly (`123456` in this example), as shown next

   ```
   jcmd 123456 \
     JFR.start \
     name='Start-JFR' \
     duration=30s \
     filename='./jfr/demo-jcmd.jfr'
   ```

   Make sure that the directories (`./jfr` in this example) where the JFR file
   (`demo-jcmd.jfr` in this example) is saved exists, as otherwise the
   application will fail to start.

4. (*Optional*) Check the recording status

   You can check the status of the recording using the `JFR.check` option

   ```shell
   PID="$(cat './target/start-jfr-jcmd.pid')"
   jcmd "${PID}" JFR.check
   ```

   If the recording is still running, the output will be similar to the
   following.

   ```
   123456:
   Recording 1: name=Start-JFR duration=30s (running)
   ```

   If the recording has finished, then the output will be similar to the
   following.

   ```
   No available recordings.

   Use jcmd 123456 JFR.start to start a recording.
   ```

   Alternatively, you can simply wait 30 seconds for the recording to finish.

   ```shell
   sleep 30
   ```

5. (*Optional*) Verify that the file was created as expected

   ```shell
   tree --sort=name './jfr'
   ```

   The recording

   ```
   ./jfr
   └── demo-jcmd.jfr

   1 directory, 1 file
   ```

6. Close the application when ready

   No need to keep the application running once the dump has been generated.

   ```shell
   kill "$(cat './target/start-jfr-jcmd.pid')"
   ```

7. Open the recording file (`./jfr/demo-jcmd.jfr`), in JDK Mission Control

   ```shell
   jmc -open "$(pwd)/jfr/demo-jcmd.jfr"
   ```

## Start JFR when starting the application

1. Start the application using the `-XX:StartFlightRecording` option.

   While it is not important to run the application in the background, it’s
   convenient as you don’t have to switch to another terminal window.

   ```shell
   java \
     -XX:StartFlightRecording=duration=30s,name=Start-JFR,filename='./jfr/demo-cla.jfr' \
     -jar './target/libs/start-jfr-1.0.0.jar' > './target/start-jfr-cla.log' 2>&1 &

   # Save the PID so later steps can reuse it after this entry finishes.
   echo "$!" > './target/start-jfr-cla.pid'
   ```

   The application will run until interrupted (killed).

2. Wait 30 seconds for the recording to complete

   ```shell
   sleep 30
   ```

3. (*Optional*) Verify that the file was created as expected

   ```shell
   tree --sort=name './jfr'
   ```

   The recordings

   ```
   ./jfr
   ├── demo-cla.jfr
   └── demo-jcmd.jfr

   1 directory, 2 files
   ```

4. Close the application when ready

   No need to keep the application running once the dump has been generated.

   ```shell
   kill "$(cat './target/start-jfr-cla.pid')"
   ```

5. Open the recording file (`./jfr/demo-cla.jfr`), in JDK Mission Control

   ```shell
   jmc -open "$(pwd)/jfr/demo-cla.jfr"
   ```

## Start JFR programmatically

The flight recording can be started programmatically, as shown in the following
code fragment. Note that the `Recording` takes a `Configuration`, and we are
using the default configuration. We will come back to this at a later stage. For
the time being just note that JFR is very customizable, and we can collect the
data we need at the level we need it. The default configuration provides the
right balance between amount of information and performance overhead (under 1%),
which makes it ideal for production use.

```java
try (Recording recording = new Recording(Configuration.getConfiguration("default"))) {
    recording.setDestination(Path.of("./jfr/demo-programmatically.jfr"));
    recording.setName("Start-JFR");
    recording.setDuration(Duration.ofSeconds(30));
    recording.start();

    /* Wait while capturing the events and saved the to the recording. */
    System.out.println("The application will terminate automatically in about 40 seconds");
    TimeUnit.SECONDS.sleep(40);
}
/* The recording is completed and written to file. */
/* No more events are captured by this recording. */
```

1. Update the code

   Copy the updated version of the code from the `fixtures/01-programmatically/`
   directory.

   ```shell
   rsync --archive 'fixtures/01-programmatically/' .
   ```

   The [`Main` class](./src/main/java/demo/Main.java) should look like the
   following example.

   ```java
   package demo;

   import module java.base;
   import module jdk.jfr;

   import jdk.jfr.Configuration;

   public final class Main {

       static void main() throws Exception {
           try (Recording recording = new Recording(Configuration.getConfiguration("default"))) {
               recording.setDestination(Path.of("./jfr/demo-programmatically.jfr"));
               recording.setName("Start-JFR");
               recording.setDuration(Duration.ofSeconds(30));
               recording.start();

               /* Wait while capturing the events and saved the to the recording. */
               System.out.println("The application will terminate automatically in about 40 seconds");
               TimeUnit.SECONDS.sleep(40);
           }
           /* The recording is completed and written to file. */
           /* No more events are captured by this recording. */
       }
   }
   ```

2. Rebuild the application

   ```shell
   ./mvnw clean package
   ```

3. Run the application without providing any JFR related options.

   While it is not important to run the application in the background, it’s
   convenient as you don’t have to switch to another terminal window.

   ```shell
   java -jar './target/libs/start-jfr-1.0.0.jar' > './target/output.txt' 2>&1
   ```

   The application will simply wait 40 seconds, and it will then exist.

4. (*Optional*) Verify that the file was created as expected

   ```shell
   tree --sort=name './jfr'
   ```

   The recordings

   ```
   ./jfr
   ├── demo-cla.jfr
   ├── demo-jcmd.jfr
   └── demo-programmatically.jfr

   1 directory, 3 files
   ```

5. Open the recording file (`./jfr/demo-programmatically.jfr`), in JDK Mission
   Control

   ```shell
   jmc -open "$(pwd)/jfr/demo-programmatically.jfr"
   ```

## Start JFR through Java Management Service (JMS)

JFR can be started for any Java application that is captured by the
[Java Management Service](https://docs.oracle.com/en-us/iaas/jms/index.html).
For more information about this option, please visit
[this article](https://docs.oracle.com/en-us/iaas/jms/doc/run-jdk-flight-recorder.html).
